questions.question: What are clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation?

seeded.answer:
Clinicians identify documentation burden as their number one contributor to burnout, with 52% of physicians specifically citing it as a major factor [1][2].

64% of physicians report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours, averaging 1.2 hours per day [1][2].

sources.title: Survey — Clinician Burnout & Documentation Burden Baseline
sources.excerpt:
[HIGH] (documentation as burnout driver) Documentation burden ranked as the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%).
[MEDIUM] (after-hours charting) 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day.

sources.title: Clinician Experience & Documentation Burden
sources.excerpt: Documentation burden is real and quantifiable, not just anecdotal. The September baseline found documentation burden is physicians' #1 self-selected burnout driver (52%, ahead of patient volume at 31%), with 64% doing regular after-hours "pajama time" charting (avg. 1.2 hrs/day). This is now the official pre-AI baseline for measuring Compass AI's impact at 6 and 12 months post-GA. Caveat: the September survey mentioned the AI initiative explicitly in its framing, while the February survey didn't — any comparison between the two datasets needs to account for that framing difference, not treat them as a clean before/after.

questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?

seeded.answer:
Physicians in v0.1 of the Ambient Scribe were skeptical and read every generated line because medication dosage errors were present in 3 of 5 sessions. [1] This reinforced their caution. [1]

Physicians also said that medication dosage errors were disqualifying for direct sign-off without review. [2]

sources.title: The Longitudinal Physician — Ambient Scribe Journey (v0.1 to Post-GA)
sources.excerpt:
v0.1 (Feb 2025) — Skeptical, reads every generated line; medication dosage errors present in 3 of 5 sessions reinforce that caution.
v0.2 (Sep 2025) — Errors drop, but reading behavior doesn't — still reads every line despite the accuracy gain. A frustration plateau: "why doesn't this feel any different?"
GA Candidate (Jan 2026) — Per-line confidence highlighting introduces the first behavior change: begins skimming high-confidence lines for the first time. Relief, tempered by sound-alike medication names still being a known, monitored gap.

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient AI Scribe Prototype v0.1
sources.excerpt:
[CRITICAL] (phi-handling) In 2 of 5 sessions, the prototype's draft transcript persisted in an editable state after the simulated encounter ended with no clear indication of where/how long it was stored — a potential PHI retention/audit gap that needs Security review before any real-patient pilot.
[HIGH] (accuracy) The scribe correctly captured the chief complaint and HPI in all 5 sessions but missed or garbled medication dosages in 3 of 5 — physicians said this was disqualifying for direct sign-off without review.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the AI's citations?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted the AI to provide inline citations that linked to the specific chart text behind each suggestion, rather than just a black-box draft. [1][2]

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

sources.title: Prior Authorization Drafting Panel
sources.excerpt: Inline source citations (the citation-expanded state) were added directly in response to the 2025-04-08 v1 testing finding that nurses wanted to see the chart text behind each suggestion. Validated as actively used, not ignored, in 2025-11-04 v2 testing.

questions.question: How did new admins expect the invite step to work?

seeded.answer: New admins were unsure whether invites would send immediately or only when the setup process was finished. [1][2]

sources.title: Onboarding Study — Session 1–3 Topline
sources.excerpt:
All 3 participants paused at step 4 ("Invite your team") — unsure whether invites send immediately or wait until setup is finished.
2 of 3 tried to skip step 3 ("Connect calendar") entirely, assuming it was optional even though it's required.
Nobody read the sidebar progress indicator — all navigated by scrolling.

sources.title: Dana's Monday Morning Setup
sources.excerpt:
Dana opens the signup link from an email, still reading a Slack message.
She breezes through steps 1–3 (signup, basics, calendar), barely reading.
Step 4 ("Invite your team") — she stops, phone buzzes, she hesitates before adding real emails.
She adds one test email first to see what happens (current design gives her no way to do this safely).
Relief when nothing sends immediately — but she wasn't sure until then.

questions.question: What evidence supports making the calendar step required in onboarding?

seeded.answer:
The onboarding usability sessions showed that participants tried to skip the calendar connection step.
- 2 of 3 participants in sessions 1-3 attempted to skip step 3 outright, assuming it was optional even though it's required [1][2].
- Participant in session 1 paused at step 3 and said "wait, do I have to do this?" before proceeding [3].
The funnel export from January 2026 shows step 3 as the largest drop-off point in the wizard [1].

sources.title: Onboarding Flow — Q1 Readout
sources.excerpt: Across all 6 onboarding usability sessions (Jan 19-23, 2026), the single largest source of first-time-setup friction is step 3 ("Connect calendar") reading as optional when it's actually required — 2 of 3 participants in sessions 1-3 attempted to skip it outright, and sessions 4-6 read it as optional in the same way. This is independently corroborated by the Jan 2026 funnel export, which shows step 3 as the largest drop-off point in the wizard.

questions.question: What is unresolved about the session timeout?

seeded.answer:
The interaction of the locked state with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. [1]

The raw notes don't say whether the 10-minute idle timeout policy settles this dispute or is a separate idle-lock setting. [2]

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
sources.excerpt: Session lock during active dictation currently reads as silent data loss, even though it isn't. The locked state's interaction with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.
